extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, inventors, and patent examiners (persons preparing or prosecuting patent applications)
extracted.subtask_short: filing and examination of patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing, filing, and prosecuting U.S. patent applications: requirements for models and specimens, what constitutes filing, formal requirements, division of applications, examination on form and merits, and rules for rejection notices and references. Useful to applicants and examiners managing application procedure and evidence of patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model not Filed until Ordered by the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: A model is not required until an examination of the application in the Patent Office shows it to be necessary to the full disclosure of the essential characteristics of the invention. When thus required, notice to that effect is sent to the applicant and proceedings on his application are suspended until it is furnished. A model filed, when not required, is returned to the inventor. No model of a design is requisite where it can be sufficiently represented by photographs or drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner decides a model is useful it will be ordered and prosecution suspended until furnished; if a model is filed voluntarily when not required it will be returned. Photographs or drawings may suffice for design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model: its General Requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: A model must clearly exhibit every feature of the invention which forms the subject of a Claim, but should not include any other matter than that covered by the actual invention, unless it be necessary to the representation of the invention in a working model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working model often desirable to show precise operation. Model must be neatly and substantially made of durable material (metal preferred) unless material is an essential feature. Size, finish, and other minor requisites must conform to Patent Office regulations; sufficiency is conclusively determined by the Office. A model should not include unrelated matter except as necessary for representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model: its Final Disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is rejected in the Patent Office, and more than two years have elapsed since such rejection, the model will be returned to the applicant upon demand, at his expense, unless it is deemed necessary to preserve it in the Office. When an applicant formally abandons a pending application and files a certificate to that effect, duly signed by him, the model will be restored. Where a patent is granted, the model remains permanently in the Patent Office, and cannot be removed therefrom except in the custody of some sworn employee of the Office, authorized for that purpose by the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models may be returned or retained according to procedural status; applicants should expect models to remain with PTO when patent issues and removal subject to strict custody rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model: its Relation to other Parts of the Application
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing of a model does not constitute the filing of an application, nor is it any evidence that the application is complete. Each portion of the application must be judged by itself. A sufficient model does not validate an imperfect Description nor an improper Claim, nor supply the place of an accurate drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A model corresponds with the specification and drawings only so far as it adheres to established rules; it cannot cure defective written disclosure or improper claims. Filing a model alone will not start prosecution or substitute for required papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimens instead of Drawings or Model (compositions of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition of matter not being capable of representation by drawings or model, the law requires the applicant to forward to the Patent Office, on the request of the Commissioner, such specimens of the ingredients and of the composition as will be sufficient for the purpose of experimentally showing the essential features of the invention. In all cases where the article is not perishable, a specimen of the composition claimed, put up in proper form to be preserved by the Office, must be furnished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For chemical or material inventions that cannot be shown by drawing/model, furnish specimens sufficient for experimental showing; non-perishable items must be packaged for preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of Application is the Commencement of Proceedings to Obtain a Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The act by which the attention of the Patent Office is directed to the claims of the inventor, and his right to an examination of those claims is secured, is the filing of the application with the Commissioner of Patents. This may be done at any time after the invention is completed, provided no abandonment has taken place; but until it is done the Office can take no notice of the invention further than to allow the inventor access to its library, records, and models, and to supply him with such copies of them as he may desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing brings the application into the Office's process; before filing the Office will only provide access to materials, not recognition of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing of Application: in What it Consists
rubrics_metrics.description: An application is filed when the petition, oath, and specification are presented in writing to the Commissioner, accompanied by such drawings as the nature of the case admits, and by such model or specimens as the Commissioner may himself require. Neither the filing of a model, nor the writing of an application, nor the placing of the case in the hands of an attorney with instructions to apply for a patent, constitutes the filing of an application. Nor is an application filed until all its parts have been received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All required parts should be presented together; if not, each part must include a letter accurately connecting it to previously filed parts. An application not completed by presentation of all parts within two years of lodging the petition is regarded as abandoned unless the delay was unavoidable (Commissioner's decision on reasonableness is conclusive). Signing or delivering incomplete papers or giving instructions to counsel is not sufficient to effect filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application once Filed known by Date and Number
rubrics_metrics.description: When all the required parts of an application have been thus presented, it is placed on file for examination and a serial number given it, notice of which is sent to the applicant. Thenceforth the application is known both to the Office and to the inventor by its number, as well as by the title of the invention, and in all his correspondence with the Office concerning it, the inventor or his attorney must define the subject-matter of his communication by stating the name of the applicant, the title of the invention, the serial number of the application, and the date when it was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the serial number/date/title/applicant name in all communications to identify and avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application once Filed not Withdrawn; Preserved in Secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: After an application is completed, the specification cannot be withdrawn from the Patent Office for any purpose whatever, though the model or the drawing may be returned to the applicant for such corrections as are deemed necessary. A copy of the specification may, however, be obtained by the inventor or his attorney. From all other persons outside of the department every part of the application is preserved in secrecy, and no information is given concerning it to any one without due authority from the inventor, except in interference cases, or when the application has been rejected or abandoned, and in the judgment of the Commissioner its disclosure may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants cannot retrieve the specification once filed; confidentiality is maintained except in statutorily or Commissioner-authorized situations (interferences, rejections, abandonment with disclosure deemed necessary). Models/drawings may be returned for correction but not the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of Fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The payment of the fees required by law is made by statute a condition of the issue of the patent, and the rules of the Patent Office prescribe their payment in advance, though when a patent issues before compliance with this requisite, it is not on that account invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees may be paid to the Commissioner, Treasurer, Assistant Treasurers, designated depositaries, or by postal order/money mailed. Receipts transmitted to the PTO accepted as evidence. Money paid by mistake or in excess will be refunded. Payment is a statutory condition for issuance, but late compliance does not necessarily invalidate an issued patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of Application: Objections to Its Form
rubrics_metrics.description: On the receipt of any application in the Office, and the payment of the fee, it is assigned to its proper class, and when its turn arrives is first subjected to an examination to determine whether it is in all respects in proper form. If found to be formally sufficient, an examination into the merits of the application, and the patentability of the invention therein claimed, is instituted. But if decided to be insufficient the applicant is notified of the defect, and such information is given to him as will enable him to judge of the propriety of the decision, and, if possible, to correct his error. Upon this notice he may either supply the alleged defect, or he may insist upon the sufficiency of the application and file a written request for a reconsideration, distinctly and specifically pointing out the errors in the finding of the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all formal objections and reasons (preferably in first letter); formal matters should be settled before rejecting claims on the merits. Applicant may request reconsideration or appeal. An examiner may consider merits despite form defects only if he gives the applicant sufficient information to remove the defects and states formal objections as required. The PTO must act as a friend to the applicant and aid in securing the actual invention when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misjoinder and Division of the Application
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single application embraces several independent inventions in violation of the rules regarding the joinder of inventions, the applicant will be required to limit his present application to some one of them, and may then file separate applications for the others. If the independence of the inventions is clear on the face of the application, this division must be ordered before any examination on the merits; if not clear, the division may be required at any time when its necessity becomes evident before final action. Whether a division shall be made rests entirely within the judgment of the Patent Office, but none should be ordered unless each of the alleged independent inventions would be a proper subject-matter for a separate patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Division should be ordered only after sufficient examination to show necessity; the examiner must clearly point out the nature and extent of the required division to enable filing separate applications. Divisions between separable parts of the same machine must not cover the same ground; divisions between process and product require pointing out other processes if relied upon. Election is not binding until applicant complies and Office accepts action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional Application Formalities and Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The division is effected by an amendment of the original application, confining its Claims, and so far as practicable its Description, to a single invention, and the filing of such additional applications for the other inventions as may be deemed advisable. These additional applications are so far independent of the original that each must be attested by a new oath, and possess all the other prerequisites of a complete application; when the patents are allowed, the date of the original application is regarded as the date of all the others, in reference to the questions of priority and public use, in order that the rights of the inventor to his entire invention, as first applied for, may be fully preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional applications cannot be based on new matter added after filing. Where divisions relate to same general subject-matter, cross-disclaimers and references should be used. Each divisional needs new oath and complete requirements; all divisional applications bear the original filing date for priority purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and Specimens may be Ordered During Merits Examination
rubrics_metrics.description: No preliminary examination of the application is made in the Patent Office to ascertain whether or not a model will be necessary. The application, if complete in other respects, is subjected to an examination on its merits, and if in the course of this examination it appears to the examiner that a model will be useful, an order to furnish one is sent to the applicant, and proceedings are suspended until the order is obeyed. The same rule applies to specimens of a composition and of its ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be prepared to furnish models/specimens upon examiner request during merits examination; prosecution will be suspended until compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination on Merits: Questions to be Determined
rubrics_metrics.description: This examination consists in an inquiry into the legal right of the applicant to a patent for the invention described and claimed in the application. It involves two questions: (1) Whether the subject-matter of the application is, in itself, a patentable invention; (2) Whether the applicant or his decedent was its true and first inventor. The former question is divisible into five subordinate ones: (1) Whether the subject-matter of the application is the result of a true and complete inventive act; (2) Whether it is embraced in either one of the six classes of inventions which are made patentable by the act of Congress; (3) Whether it is new; (4) Whether it is useful; (5) Whether it has been abandoned to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In uncontested cases the oath is prima facie proof of priority; the examiner is not bound by strict rules of evidence but must ascertain as best he can from publications, patents, and general knowledge whether to allow or reject. The examiner must follow Commissioner's decisions and court rules. If patentable and inventor is true/first inventor, allowance; if not, rejection; if doubt, decision either way to permit reconsideration/appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Application: Notice and References
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application, or one of the Claims in an application, is rejected upon any ground whatever the examiner is required to notify the applicant of such rejection, stating all his reasons therefor fully and precisely, and giving him such information and references as may assist him in judging of the advisability of prosecuting his application or of altering his specification. If the ground of the rejection be that the applicant is not the true and first inventor of the art or instrument described, the examiner must cite references establishing his assertion, or himself make oath to it, to overcome the presumption arising from the oath of the alleged inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejection is for lack of novelty, the examiner must disclose all his information citing the best references: prior patents (date, number, patentee, class), prior publications (title, date, page/plate, place where copy may be procured), and any factual references supported by affidavit. Pertinence must be clearly explained and the anticipated Claim particularly specified. Devices cited need not have commercial value nor be identical in form, material, or mode of use—substantial correspondence suffices. An abandoned or rejected application is generally not a public document for prior knowledge, and the examiner is not obliged to suggest proper claims; all references and objections should be cited on or before final rejection (though late-discovered references may be urged promptly thereafter).
